title: Design Linked List
description:
# Design Linked List

Design a `MyLinkedList` class that stores integers and supports index-based access, insertion, and deletion. The list is 0-indexed: the head node is index `0`, the next node is index `1`, and so on.

Implement the `MyLinkedList` class:

* `MyLinkedList()` Initializes an empty list.
* `int get(int index)` Returns the value at `index`. If `index` is outside the current list, return `-1`.
* `void addAtHead(int val)` Inserts `val` before the current first element.
* `void addAtTail(int val)` Appends `val` after the current last element.
* `void addAtIndex(int index, int val)` Inserts `val` before the node currently at `index`. If `index == length`, append to the tail. If `index > length`, do nothing.
* `void deleteAtIndex(int index)` Deletes the node at `index` if it exists.

You may implement a singly linked list, a doubly linked list, or another manual sequence representation. Do not use Java's built-in `LinkedList`.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1

**Input:**
["MyLinkedList", "addAtHead", "addAtTail", "addAtIndex", "get", "deleteAtIndex", "get"]
[[], [1], [3], [1, 2], [1], [1], [1]]

**Output:**
[null, null, null, null, 2, null, 3]

**Explanation:**
`addAtHead(1)` creates `[1]`; `addAtTail(3)` creates `[1,3]`; `addAtIndex(1,2)` creates `[1,2,3]`; `get(1)` returns `2`; after deleting index `1`, the list is `[1,3]`, so `get(1)` returns `3`.

## Constraints

* `0 <= index, val <= 1000`
* At most `2000` calls are made to `get`, `addAtHead`, `addAtTail`, `addAtIndex`, and `deleteAtIndex`.
* Do not use Java's built-in `LinkedList` class.

solutions.name: Singly Linked List with Dummy Head
solutions.timeComplexity: get/addAtIndex/deleteAtIndex O(n), addAtHead O(1), addAtTail O(n)
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep a dummy head node before the first real node and a size counter. For indexed insert/delete, walk to the predecessor of the target position and then change one `next` pointer.

## Key Insight

The dummy head makes operations at index `0` look the same as operations in the middle: there is always a predecessor node to edit.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: `get`, `addAtIndex`, and `deleteAtIndex` are O(n); `addAtHead` is O(1); `addAtTail` delegates to index `size`, so it is O(n).
- Space Complexity: O(n) nodes.

solutions.name: Doubly Linked List with Head and Tail Sentinels
solutions.timeComplexity: O(min(index, n-index)) for indexed access, O(1) for head/tail insertion
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep dummy head and tail sentinels around all real nodes. Each node stores `prev` and `next`, and `nodeAt` starts from the closer end before inserting or deleting.

## Key Insight

Two sentinels remove empty-list and tail-edge special cases, while backward links let high indices be reached from the tail.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: Indexed operations take O(min(index, n-index)); head and tail insertion are O(1).
- Space Complexity: O(n) nodes.

solutions.name: Singly Linked List with Tail Pointer
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use a dummy head plus a `tail` pointer. Tail insertion links directly after `tail`, while deletion updates `tail` when the removed node was the last real node.

## Key Insight

A singly linked list cannot walk backward, so the tail pointer only makes appends O(1); deleting by index still needs the predecessor.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: `addAtHead` and `addAtTail` are O(1); indexed access, indexed insertion, and indexed deletion are O(n).
- Space Complexity: O(n) nodes.

solutions.name: Dynamic Array Backed Sequence
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store values in a resizable `int[]`. `get` is direct indexing; insertion shifts the suffix one step right, and deletion shifts the suffix one step left.

## Key Insight

This is not a linked list, but it is a useful manual baseline: arrays trade cheap indexed reads for expensive middle edits.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: `get` is O(1); insertions and deletions are O(n).
- Space Complexity: O(n).

solutions.name: Cursor Linked List with Arrays
solutions.description:
## Approach

Represent nodes by integer slots in arrays: `value[slot]`, `prev[slot]`, and `next[slot]`. Slots `0` and `1` are head and tail sentinels, and every insertion allocates `nextFree++`.

## Key Insight

A linked list is about links, not object allocation. Array cursors give the same predecessor/successor operations with compact integer storage.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: Indexed operations are O(min(index, n-index)); head and tail insertion are O(1).
- Space Complexity: O(number of inserted nodes) array slots.

tests.description: Canonical operations insert in the middle and then delete that middle node.
Out-of-range insert/delete are ignored; index equal to size appends.
Delete middle, head, and tail positions while preserving remaining order.
Alternating head and tail insertions produce the expected full order.
Appending through addAtIndex(size, val) still works after deleting the tail.
Deleting the only node returns the structure to an empty reusable state.
Repeated middle insertions keep all following nodes linked in order.
Accessing both ends after deleting the tail catches stale tail and size bugs.
Deleting from an empty list is ignored, and index zero append works after a full clear.
